title: Layer-selective and magnetic-field-enhanced transport of topological kink states in rhombohedral multilayer graphene
abstract: Topological valley kink states (VKSs), which are quantum valley Hall states emerging at the interfaces between adjacent domains with opposite valley Chern numbers, have attracted considerable interest in graphene-based systems. In this work, we investigate the quantum transport of VKSs in ABC-stacked rhombohedral multilayer graphene in the presence of Anderson disorder and a perpendicular magnetic field. Two prominent transport characteristics are revealed. First, in the absence of a magnetic field, the kink states exhibit strong layer polarization, with their wave functions predominantly localized and equally distributed on the outermost top and bottom layers. As a result, their transport properties are highly sensitive to the layer-selective disorder distribution. Second, under a perpendicular magnetic field, the layer-symmetric spatial distribution of VKSs is broken, leading to a significant reduction in the wave-function overlap between counter-propagating VKSs from opposite valleys. Consequently, intervalley scattering is suppressed, and the transmission of VKSs through disordered regions is substantially enhanced. Our results provide new insights into multichannel topological valley transport in rhombohedral multilayer graphene and demonstrates disorder-engineering and magnetic fields as effective approaches for manipulating the propagation of VKSs.
summary: This work theoretically examines how topological valley kink states behave in multilayer graphene under disorder and a magnetic field. The key finding is that applying a perpendicular magnetic field breaks symmetry, which effectively suppresses backscattering between opposite valleys. This demonstrates that magnetic fields and disorder engineering are powerful tools for controlling topological transport in graphene nanostructures.
main_problem: The study investigates the quantum transport of Topological Valley Kink States (VKSs) in rhombohedral multilayer graphene (RMG) when subjected to Anderson disorder and a perpendicular magnetic field.
main_result: The perpendicular magnetic field breaks layer symmetry, suppressing intervalley backscattering and significantly enhancing the transmission of VKSs through disordered regions. Furthermore, the transport is highly sensitive to the layer-selective distribution of disorder.
method: The analysis employs numerical Landauer-Büttiker conductance calculations based on a tight-binding model Hamiltonian, supplemented by low-energy continuum descriptions for topological invariants.
model_or_system: The system is ABC-stacked rhombohedral multilayer graphene (RMG) modeled by a tight-binding Hamiltonian incorporating nearest-neighbor hopping, layer-dependent electrostatic potentials, and disorder terms. The perpendicular magnetic field is included via the Peierls substitution.
key_observables: Conductance ($\langle G angle$), wave function localization, intervalley scattering suppression, and the valley Chern number ($C_{\xi}$).
important_parameters: Perpendicular magnetic field strength ($\mathbf{B}_{\perp}$), disorder strength/distribution, and the number of graphene layers ($N$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes an armchair edge termination for the ribbon geometry and utilizes low-energy continuum descriptions near the Dirac points.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic transport device, layer-polarized wave function distributions, band structures showing VKSs, and conductance measurements comparing results with and without a magnetic field.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the model for VKSs in RMG, then analyzes the transport behavior in the absence of a magnetic field (showing layer polarization), and finally details how the perpendicular magnetic field breaks symmetry to enhance transport by suppressing intervalley scattering.
why_interesting: The control mechanisms identified—layer-selective disorder and magnetic fields—provide concrete, tunable knobs for manipulating topological edge state transport, which is relevant for designing robust quantum interconnects or novel electronic devices.
